meaning: Titles and reading notes drafted by an AI agent in the register of the paper they annotate. No mathematician has reviewed them.

notes.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CellSystemCond: These fifteen conditions concern shared fields, derivatives, matrices and uniform bounds. A checking program must separately prove that its decoded data satisfy all of them.
notes.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CertificateCla: The inequalities leave the numerical constants and the parameter family unspecified. The decimal bounds in the digest are arithmetic consequences of the paper’s chosen constants, rather than verified margins for a supplied instance.
notes.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isExtendedCert: The cell conditions yield a certificate after choosing a sufficiently large common decay bound. The argument also uses the established field, offset, reference-error and adjoint reduction results.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.HH: The forcing is represented as a square-integrable time-periodic solenoidal Fourier field. The Leray projection and the physical representation identify the part of a physical forcing that acts on solenoidal tests.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.Internal.AtProfile.coerci: Absorbing the reference-field error divides the L² and pin constants by 1−ϑ and the row weights by (1−ϑ)². The resulting estimate applies at the approximate profile itself.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedBordered: The finite-dimensional identity can be added and subtracted inside the compact perturbation. Thus the full bordered operator, including the force and pin blocks, has the Fredholm form needed to deduce surjectivity from injectivity.
This result retains a continuous periodic curve of gradients in the homogeneous energy space. Taking its squared norm gives the continuous scalar enstrophy used in the integrated energy identity.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.XX: The complete iteration space controls the two spatial derivative norms. Each bordered solve supplies the additional time equation required for membership in D_S.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.extendedAdjointEnclosureH: The adjoint enclosure is proved after setting the multiplier weight to one. The preceding rescaling of force fields and coefficients transports a general positive multiplier weight to this normalization.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.extendedAdjointPairingHol: At zero perturbation, the adjoint-defect condition annihilates every gradient forcing. Hence the adjoint equals its solenoidal projection, which makes its pairing with an equation modulo gradients well defined.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.extendedDataContinuityHol: The continuity argument uses residual pairings with compact solenoidal tests. The chosen residual need not vary continuously in the H norm.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.extendedExistsZeroHeldHol: Parameter selection is carried out after reference-field absorption and multiplier normalization. At that stage the reference and approximate fields agree, the multiplier weight is one, and both transfer shifts vanish.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.extendedHeldContractsHold: Condition (7.26) controls the supremum part of the difference distance. The paper’s simultaneous Schauder–Tychonoff proof does not use this condition.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.extendedHeldExistsUniqueH: Uniqueness holds for the bounded nonlinear corrections at one fixed parameter after normalization. It does not select a unique parameter or a unique periodic profile among all solutions.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.extendedHeldLimitHolds_of: The limit argument passes nonlinear bounded corrections to a correction at the limiting parameter. The paper instead passes linear solves indexed by an independent quadratic-force variable to a limit.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.extendedHeldMapsToHolds_o: At a fixed parameter, the nonlinear update preserves both the weighted correction radius and the gradient-supremum budget. The paper organizes its bounds as a simultaneous map of the parameter and an independent forcing variable.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.extendedHeldNonzeroHolds_: The gradient lower bound rules out a corrected field that vanishes almost everywhere in space and time. After choosing its smooth representative, this yields pointwise nontriviality.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.extendedSigmaProfileOfHel: The construction adds the selected correction to the approximate profile and uses its parameter-dependent period. Its final existence conclusion omits the chosen parameter, pins and correction bounds.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.extendedStiffEnclosureHol: The complementary-coordinate estimate is proved after multiplier normalization. Combining it with the approximate-field offset gives the weighted-ball part of the parameter enclosure.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.extendedSupBoundHolds_of: The shorter period is required only for scalar enstrophy. The forcing representative can have period one, which is sufficient for the full-period averaging argument.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.freeEnergyLocalHolds_of: The enstrophy identity is integrated over a time interval and uses a continuous periodic scalar representative. Its differential form holds wherever that scalar representative is differentiable.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.heldDist: The distance combines the weighted correction norm and a scaled essential gradient supremum. Closedness of the bounded correction class and the required limit properties are established before applying the contraction argument.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.productBoundHolds_of: The product estimate controls both the physical convection field and its solenoidal projection. It uses the essential time supremum, which agrees with the ordinary supremum for the continuous homogeneous-space representative.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.readingEnergyHolds_of: The physical energy uses the Frobenius square of the gradient and the trace of a weak Hessian. Their agreement with the derivative-space norm uses the closed spatial derivative relation.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.sizeZ: The joint norm here uses multiplier weight one. Rescaling the force fields and their coefficients restores the general weight ω, while retaining the physical spatial weight w.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.pivotCoun: The pivot argument gives a positive subspace for the root form. Positivity of the total leaf form on that same subspace follows by the separate tree lower bound.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.signedTre: Telescoping retains the root-front quadratic form together with the pivot gains and negative column squares. A nonnegative root front, positive pivot coverage and a bound on the number of columns are additional inputs to positivity.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.stateTerm: The auxiliary directions may form the graph (Lu,u), and some physical coordinates may be ignored when the form is independent of them. The dimension condition is applied after accounting for those coordinates.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.ShapeParam: The symmetry order is a natural-number parameter, with positivity required by the validity conditions elsewhere. Neither the intended value 19 nor the choice m=2 is selected by these data alone.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.angularModeB: The angular estimates hold almost everywhere for the Fourier components of weak perturbations. Besides the two displayed bounds, the result also controls curl by its gradient and relates curl energy to gradient energy.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.exteriorConditionSoun: The exterior argument distinguishes ray exteriors from a square exterior. The latter also needs zero azimuthal frequency and the relevant reflection symmetry, so the scalar Hardy inequality is only part of the hypothesis.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.labelPhase: The phase uses time frequency 2ι₂−ι₁ and azimuthal frequency ksym ι₁. These correspond to θ and φ in the digest; the height ratio uses the third Cartesian coordinate.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.RowMultiplierIneq: The multiplier inequality allows general positive coercivity and nonnegative pin coefficients. The values 3/50 and 1000 are the paper’s specialization of this algebra.
notes.Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.rec_: The forward recurrence keeps the homogeneous term generated by the initial value. On the stable component, that term records the stable part introduced by the compactly supported transversal.
notes.Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.tail: The tail series includes powers of Θ because its forcing sequence has been divided by the desired decay factor. Its inverse already acts through the exceptional projection.
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.defect: The approximate residual uses a weak Hessian and a pressure-gradient representative orthogonal to solenoidal tests. A globally classical Hessian and a chosen scalar pressure are not required at this stage.
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.target: The pin targets are prescribed for the full profile. Subtracting the approximate profile’s pins gives the correction targets used in the bordered problem.
notes.Breakdown.FarField.farFieldDecay_holds: Decay is proved from a similarity integral equation through weighted kernel bounds and derivative estimates. The result also controls the pressure gradient; it does not invoke Chae–Wolf as an external hypothesis.
notes.Breakdown.FarField.periodicLerayProfileE: The public implication retains existence of a smooth profile. The smoothing theorem preserves velocity identity for a specified mild orbit, while further transport is needed to recover the original correction, parameter, pins and bounds.
notes.Breakdown.FarField.smoothFieldOfOrbit_ho: The paper’s proof passes from L⁶ to L¹² and then L∞. The formal construction obtains a smooth representative using Fourier estimates, local mild-solution smoothing and overlapping time intervals.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.BilinSpec: The interaction is specified by all its Hilbert-space pairings. This permits the nonlinear term to be defined without taking a pointwise Fourier transform of each physical product.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.BilinExists.bili: The symmetric trilinear pairing is unchanged when its two velocity inputs are interchanged. Existence of the corresponding bounded bilinear operator and its physical heat-Leray formula are separate results.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.GradSixDecay.cut: The cutoff is smooth, equals one on the radius-R ball and vanishes outside the radius-2R ball when R > 0. Completion of the physical homogeneous Sobolev space requires the surrounding approximation argument.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.GradSixDecay.mem: Inverse-radius decay makes the sixth power integrable in three dimensions. Membership in the full homogeneous gradient space also requires gradient integrability and the embedding result.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.cutof: For each Schwartz potential and positive error tolerance, the theorem chooses one compact solenoidal approximation. Applying those choices along a sequence gives the approximation used in the exposition.
The cutoff curl is smooth, compactly supported and divergence-free. A separate convergence theorem controls both its gradient error and the gradient error of its negative Laplacian.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.symbo: The weighted curl identities hold almost everywhere, so the single frequency ξ = 0 does not affect them. The measure-zero observation is more general than this particular application.

The result constructs a Schwartz potential for each smooth annular symbol and identifies its curl at nonzero frequencies. Convergence of an approximating sequence also uses the preceding L² approximation estimates.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceDense.div_pr: The transverse projection has zero contraction with ξ, enforcing the solenoidal Fourier condition. Identifying its output with a physical divergence-free field uses the Fourier correspondence.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceDense.norm_p: The transverse projection is contractive at each frequency. Smoothness of projected symbols requires support away from zero, and the error estimate for reality averaging requires a target with the corresponding symmetry.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceDense.smooth: The smoothing result starts with an L² field already supported on a compact annulus. Truncating a general field to such annuli and passing to a convergent sequence are separate steps.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceDense.symFie: A real physical field has Fourier symmetry m(−ξ) = conjugate(m(ξ)). Averaging a symbol with its reflected conjugate imposes this symmetry.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.VelocityExists.i: Closure under addition applies once both summands are known to be compact smooth solenoidal fields. The finite-dimensional section construction supplies that property for the selected correction.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.IsWeakSolution: The weak-solution class assumes smooth decaying slices and L²-continuous time differences, in addition to the solenoidal test equation and continuity in X. The general physical weak-to-mild statement has a wider input class.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.X: The Fourier variable represents one homogeneous derivative of velocity. The continuous map into L⁶ recovers the physical velocity and fixes its additive-constant ambiguity.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.bilinCompact: The compactness proof truncates frequencies, proves total boundedness of the truncated images and controls their high-frequency tail. The Rellich argument preceding the link is the paper’s physical-space explanation.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.bilinCompact_holds: Compactness is proved for coefficients in the dense span of compact solenoidal test fields. The bilinear bound and operator-norm closure extend it to every coefficient in X.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.bilinX: The interaction is defined by its pairings with a heat-smoothed test field. The projected physical nonlinearity is identified with this operator by separate Fourier and velocity identities.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.heatDivFree: The output represents one homogeneous derivative of the physical velocity. Its multiplier therefore includes 2π|ξ| alongside the heat factor and the Leray projection; the physical Oseen tensor needs a separate identification.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.longitudinal: This is the longitudinal projection ξ⊗ξ/|ξ|². Subtracting it from the identity gives the transverse Leray projection; the real Fourier space also imposes conjugation symmetry.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.mild_holds: The formal proof obtains the mild equation from density of Fourier test fields and their Laplacians. The paper uses the cited weak-to-mild theorem for the corresponding physical argument.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.testDense_holds: Density allows the transfer argument to choose compact solenoidal initial data arbitrarily close to the profile. The formal whole-space transfer does not require the particular vector-potential cutoff displayed here.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.trilinear_holds: The proof bounds the convection pairing and then uses L² and L⁶ estimates for the smoothed test. Their combination gives the three-quarter time power without stating the displayed L³/² mapping estimate as a separate result.
notes.Breakdown.HeatBilinear.HasCompactKernel: Only compactness on a dense set of coefficients is needed for the transfer argument. The Fourier proof uses frequency restriction, equicontinuity and tail control; the physical-space proof uses local compactness of Sobolev restriction.
notes.Breakdown.Held.testSetZero_of: The raw parameter update is already proved to map K into itself. A nearest-point retraction is used only in proving the general compact-convex fixed-point theorem, after the enclosure obligation for this update has been met.
notes.Breakdown.IsPerturbation: The square-integrable transport field combines the time derivative, dilation and half the velocity before subtracting the Laplacian. The second spatial derivatives are weak derivatives.
notes.Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile: The assumption includes decay of ∇²W and ∇q. Appendix A derives those estimates analytically from the paper’s profile assumptions; that derivation is not supplied by this definition.
notes.Breakdown.MonodromyStatement: Each logarithmic period is subdivided until the linearized operator on every short interval has norm at most one quarter. The full-period map is the rotated product of the corresponding interval evolutions.
The derivative estimate concerns one similarity-profile slice and gives a bound 2C/|y| away from the origin. The physical-time version also uses the similarity change of variables.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.Cutoff.Internal.contD: The homotopy integrand is smooth in the integration parameter and spatial position for a fixed smooth field. The time-dependent application additionally tracks the smooth dependence of that field on time.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.Cutoff.Internal.hasFD: The differentiation theorem concerns the spatial parameter of an integral over [0,1]. Joint smoothness in physical time requires including that additional parameter in the argument.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.InverseAlgebra.Intern: If ‖Q‖ ≤ q < 1, the inverse of I − Q has norm at most (1 − q)⁻¹. The bound is valid on any Banach space used for the periodic inverse construction.
For an operator of norm below one, the inverse of I − Q satisfies z − Qz = y. This is the cancellation described by the convergent geometric series in the exposition.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.R3Factor: With a compact solenoidal coefficient, the linear interaction factors through the velocity and gradient restricted to its support. Approximating the recurrent coefficient by such fields is a separate step.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellData: The restricted data contain three L² gradient columns and an L⁶ velocity. Their product norm is equivalent to the local sum of norms displayed in the digest, with fixed dimension-dependent constants.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellDefs.Internal.ad: The local transport estimate includes the factor |B|¹ᐟ³ when converting L⁶ data to L² on the support ball. The full radial-extension construction and weighted-path bound need further arguments.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellTorus.Internal.e: The result is the interpolation inequality ‖f‖₃ ≤ ‖f‖₂¹ᐟ²‖f‖₆¹ᐟ². The period-uniform Sobolev inequality used after it is a separate ingredient.
The scalar estimate controls (1 + y)e⁻ʸˢ for s > 0 and y ≥ 0. The separate bound involving r¹ᐟ²e⁻ʳ needs its own elementary estimate.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellTorus.Internal.s: The duality argument treats compactly supported L² forcing after scaling to the unit torus, using the periodic Sobolev estimate and μτ ≤ 1. Extension to arbitrary L³ᐟ² forcing and all periods needs the additional physical argument.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellTorus.Internal.v: Every coordinate plane has zero three-dimensional volume. Consequently the unit-cell boundary is negligible for Fourier norm identities and for identifying the wrapping map with the identity.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup: The intermediate conclusion gives a smooth periodic datum and an unbounded periodic mild trajectory. Two-sided rates and convergence to the physical profile are additional quantitative statements.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.approxFieldProperties: The cutoff is supported on a fixed ball inside a unit-period cell and agrees with the core on a fixed smaller ball. The free radius in the paper’s presentation comes from translation and rescaling.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.approxPeriodic: Periodization uses the wrapped coordinate in a unit cube and a small blow-up time. The digest instead starts with a large-period torus and rescales it at the end.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.approxResidualSmall: The residual of the nth rescaled interval is at most K T¹/⁴ times its geometric decay factor. The digest expresses the corresponding smallness using a large torus period and a continuous weighted-time norm.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.breakdownOnTorus_of_p: The final statement excludes global smooth solutions with periodic velocity and arbitrary smooth pressure. A moving-frame argument connects that class to the periodic-pressure solutions used in the construction.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.comparisonSmall: The comparison becomes smaller than any prescribed tolerance when the blow-up time is sufficiently small. The explicit powers of the large period in the digest are conclusions of the paper’s comparison estimates.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffField: The cutoff is written as ηu+∇η×A. This is the product-rule expansion of curl(ηA) when curl A=u.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose: The estimate keeps a fixed physical cutoff near the centre of the unit torus and lets the remaining time shrink. The large-radius formulation is obtained by expressing the same geometry in similarity coordinates.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.fieldSpace: The periodic Fourier space contains the constant mode as well as the solenoidal nonzero modes. It therefore differs from the mean-zero homogeneous space used in the paper’s large-period argument.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.freeHeatComparison: For each fixed compact solenoidal field, the restricted free heat discrepancy tends uniformly to zero on a bounded time window as the scale shrinks. No explicit large-period power is included in this conclusion.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.heatDivFreeComparison: The formal projected-heat comparison is uniform on a time window [ε,ε⁻¹]. Short times are estimated separately when assembling the inverse; the paper’s Oseen argument gives explicit bounds across the full positive-time range.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyCurl: The identity holds for every smooth divergence-free spatial field and every centre. In the profile construction it is applied to each time slice.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.movingFrameReduction: A periodic velocity permits pressure with a spatially affine part. The construction removes that part by a time-dependent velocity shift and translation chosen to preserve the initial datum.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.rightInversePerturb: An operator defect of at most one half can be removed by a geometric-series inverse. The corrected right inverse has norm at most twice the original bound.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.shellInverseTransfer: The theorem eliminates the free shift, solves a reduced equation on the restriction space, and reconstructs the periodic path. Its two comparison bounds and maximum product norm must also be verified when applying it to the continuous weighted spaces.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.transplantField: The compact field is placed about (1/2,1/2,1/2) in the unit cell. A spatial translation moves that centre to the origin used in the large-torus exposition.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.transplantNorm: The periodic norm is the full H¹ norm, so the identity includes μ‖f‖²₂ in addition to ‖∇f‖²₂. The mass contribution tends to zero with μ.
notes.Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist: The profile premise also requires uniform decay of the second spatial derivative and the pressure gradient. Lemmas A.5 and A.6 explain these extra requirements analytically, but no conversion from the printed hypotheses to this premise is among the linked results.
notes.Breakdown.SmoothFlow.smooth_physField_cu: The input trajectory has every Sobolev order and satisfies its Fourier integral equation. These hypotheses give smooth physical velocity and pressure, including at the initial time; the full continuation alternative needs additional estimates.
notes.Breakdown.Spectral.exists_dichotomy: On the exceptional range, the statement gives a lower bound for forward powers and asserts surjectivity. Together these express the inverse-power decay used in the paper.
notes.Breakdown.TransferHolds: The retained conclusion is existence of arbitrarily close data in a prescribed dense space, with rescaled convergence to the orbit. The paper’s fixed finite-dimensional correction for every nearby datum is a further description of the construction.
notes.Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.integ: The scalar integral equals 4c¹ᐟ⁴. In the general Duhamel theorem, the quantitative vector bound uses t − a ≤ 1, while integrability and continuity hold on arbitrary finite intervals.
notes.Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.kern_: The assumed singular estimate is restricted to heat time at most one. On longer intervals the proof uses a bound of the form C_K(r⁻³ᐟ⁴ + 1), which still gives integrability.
notes.Breakdown.WeakProfile.weakOrbitOfParts_h: The weak-to-mild construction takes the required derivative, pairing and time-continuity results as hypotheses, supplied in the assembled proof. It concludes existence of a recurrent mild orbit without retaining the selected correction or its pins.
notes.Breakdown.breakdown_on_space: The public whole-space result excludes a global smooth solution with one energy bound for all nonnegative times. It does not return the displayed rate or profile error for a chosen singular trajectory.
notes.Breakdown.breakdown_on_torus: The public periodic result excludes a global smooth solution whose velocity is periodic. Its conclusion does not include the local H¹ comparison with a specified profile.
notes.Breakdown.compactPiece_of: The argument extends endpoint compactness from dense simple coefficients by closedness of compact operators in operator norm. The exposition gives a sequential proof of that general closedness fact.
notes.Breakdown.compactSimple_of: The proof removes the last ε of the integral and bounds that tail by a constant times ε¹/⁴. A compact convex hull controls the remainder for a simple coefficient path.
notes.Breakdown.contraction: The conclusion bounds the initial correction and returns a bounded interval sequence. Its proof chooses the correction from the first component of the right inverse, so membership in the exceptional range also requires that inverse’s range property.
notes.Breakdown.dichotomyHolds: The spectral conclusion gives two separated radii, geometric bounds and surjectivity on the finite exceptional range. Choosing a decay rate between those radii gives the weighted sums in the digest.
notes.Breakdown.exists_section: The section lifts the exceptional component into the chosen dense data space. Its values may also have a stable component, which must remain in the forward evolution.
notes.Breakdown.extended_certificate_orbit_pro: The public conclusion retains only weak-profile existence. Carrying the selected parameter, correction, pins and joint bound through smoothing requires the separately described same-witness construction.
notes.Breakdown.mildRegular_realization: The regularity theorem supplies a smooth representative with bounded energy on each fixed compact time interval. The bound by the initial energy and one bound valid on all of [0,1) are not part of this conclusion.
notes.Breakdown.mildSmallData: The small-data result gives a mild solution through time one with norm at most twice the initial norm. Scaling and interval choices supply the short-time instances needed later.
notes.Breakdown.monodromy: The formal proof subdivides a similarity period until each interval linearisation has norm at most one quarter. Identifying its endpoint product with the paper’s full-period Volterra map uses uniqueness of the linearised equation.
notes.Breakdown.orbitNorm: A slice below the small-data threshold generates a bounded solution through time one. Uniqueness and recurrence would then force the entire profile to vanish, giving the positive lower norm bound.
notes.Breakdown.orbitNorm_of: The positive lower orbit bound is proved through small-data decay, mild uniqueness and recurrence. The compact-period minimum argument in the digest is a different explanation of the same conclusion.
notes.Breakdown.orbitSeq: Each update is divided by the chosen decay factor. To obtain this recurrence from continuous forcing, first subtract the forcing path at the interval endpoints and then normalise.
notes.Breakdown.periodicInverse: The input is a bounded sequence of continuous paths on short intervals. Proposition 5.3 reconstructs the corresponding continuous weighted right inverse from this discrete mechanism.
notes.Breakdown.physicalField: The physical velocity is defined at terminal time one, with an arbitrary logarithmic phase. The formula with terminal time T follows by scaling time and space.
notes.Breakdown.physicalPressure: The pressure is defined with terminal time one and the same logarithmic phase as the physical velocity. Its multiplicative factor is (1−t)⁻¹.
notes.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: Integrability and continuity hold on every finite interval. The pure-power norm estimate requires t − a ≤ 1; the continuity proof uses a fixed integration domain and dominated convergence.
